issues.legal_issue: A presumptive reversioner’s receipt of a benefit or failure to challenge an alienation does not, without informed assent to the transaction, ratify the alienation and bar a later challenge when the reversion falls open.
material_facts: The reversioner was a minor when the widows made the settlement and was not a party to the settlement or the later transactions implementing it.

He received and enjoyed a house under the arrangement, but the evidence did not establish that he knew of his rights as a possible reversioner or understood that the widows intended to convey absolute titles.
The Collector’s certificate followed registration in the ordinary course, and the reversioner’s other conduct did not establish informed assent to the alienation.
The reversioner sued after the widow’s death to recover property alienated by her.
issues.conclusion: The reversioner had not ratified the alienation and was not precluded from challenging it; the alienation was not binding on him.
issues.legal_principle: A widow’s alienation is voidable by reversioners, who may be barred by express ratification or conduct demonstrating informed assent and election to treat the alienation as binding. Mere receipt of a benefit or failure to challenge the transaction is insufficient; whether conduct amounts to ratification is a question of fact. The Court applied Sahu Madho Das v. Pandit Mukand Ram, Dhiyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore, Kanhai Lal v. Brij Lal, Rangasami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden, and Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb.

predicates.reversioner_suit_to_avoid_widow_alienati: A person claiming as reversioner sued to avoid an alienation made by a widow of the deceased holder’s property.
predicates.reversioner_was_not_a_party: The reversioner did not participate in the transaction or arrangement that effected the alienation.
predicates.reversioner_lacked_knowledge_of_reversio: The reversioner did not know of the rights on which a later challenge as reversioner could be based.
predicates.benefit_was_only_a_gift: The reversioner received a benefit that, without further conduct, indicated assent only to that benefit and not to the wider transaction.

issues.definition: When a reversioner suing to avoid a widow’s alienation was not a party and lacked knowledge of reversionary rights or received only a gift, the reversioner is not barred by ratification.

issues.legal_issue: A settlement between a widow and her mother-in-law that is not a bona fide family arrangement does not bind a reversioner who was a minor and did not participate in it.
material_facts: The settlement was made between the widow and her mother-in-law to resolve disputes between them and allocated or provided for the disposition of the deceased holder’s properties.
The reversioner was a minor at the time and was not a party to the settlement or the transactions implementing it.
The settlement was not in the nature of a family arrangement under Hindu law.
issues.conclusion: The settlement was not binding on the reversioner.
issues.legal_principle: A presumptive reversioner who participates in a genuine family arrangement and takes a benefit under it may be precluded from disputing it when the reversion falls open; the arrangement must actually be a family arrangement, and participation or informed assent matters. The Court relied on the principles discussed in Sahu Madho Das v. Pandit Mukand Ram, Dhiyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore, Kanhai Lal v. Brij Lal, Rangasami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden, and Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb.

predicates.reversioner_suit_to_avoid_settlement_aff: A person claiming as reversioner challenged a settlement affecting the deceased holder’s property after the reversion fell open.
predicates.settlement_was_not_a_family_arrangement: The settlement resolved a dispute between others but was not a bona fide family arrangement.
predicates.reversioner_was_a_minor_nonparticipant: The reversioner was a minor and did not participate in the settlement.

issues.definition: A settlement that is not a bona fide family arrangement does not bind a reversioner who was a minor and did not participate when the reversioner later challenges it.

issues.legal_issue: An alienation by a widow is not justified by legal necessity when the transaction is made to implement a settlement and its consideration is not shown to meet legal necessity.
material_facts: The widow had obtained letters of administration subject to a restriction on dealing with the property without the required sanction.
The transfer document purported to implement the earlier settlement and did not purport to be founded on legal necessity.

Of the stated consideration, only a portion represented debts of the deceased; other identified items included document-execution expenses and funeral expenses, and the remaining items did not purport to meet legal necessity.
issues.conclusion: The transfer was not justified by legal necessity and was not binding on the reversioner.
issues.legal_principle: A widow’s alienation must be supported by legal necessity to bind the reversioner; amounts paid for purposes that do not constitute legal necessity do not establish that justification. The Court also considered the restriction attached to the letters of administration and the terms of the transfer document.

predicates.reversioner_suit_to_avoid_widow_alienati: A person claiming as reversioner sued to avoid an alienation made by a widow of the deceased holder’s property.
predicates.alienation_implemented_settlement: The transfer was made to carry out an earlier settlement between the widow and another person.
predicates.consideration_not_shown_to_meet_legal_ne: The stated payments were not shown to be for purposes that legally justified the widow’s alienation.

issues.definition: When a reversioner challenges a widow’s transfer made to implement a settlement and the consideration is not shown to meet legal necessity, the transfer is not justified by legal necessity.
